title: Tests for newer fault models
summary: March C− was designed for the classical fault models. Smaller technologies brought faults it cannot see: deceptive read faults, write-disturb faults, linked and dynamic faults. This topic shows the tests built for them — and the price paid in test length.
objectives: Explain why March C− misses DRDF and WDF.
Read March SS and say which operation catches which fault.
Describe linked and dynamic faults and the tests that target them.
Compare March tests by length and fault coverage.

blocks.md: Look at March C− again: {⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇑(r1, w0); ⇓(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0); ⇕(r0)}. Two patterns are **missing**:

rows: Two reads of a cell **with no write in between**
**DRDF** — the read returns the right value but flips the cell
Every read in March C− is followed by a write to the same cell, which overwrites the flipped value before anyone sees it.
A write of the value the cell **already holds**
**WDF** — a non-transition write flips the cell
Every write in M1–M4 changes the cell (0 → 1 or 1 → 0).
Operations **back to back** in special orders
**dynamic** faults, e.g. a write immediately followed by a read
March C− has only r-w pairs, never w-r or r-r.
blocks.caption: Gaps of March C−

blocks.title: Why it matters now
blocks.md: In nanometre SRAMs, weak cells and process variation make **read and write disturb** faults common. Industrial studies found faults that March C− lets through — which is why newer tests were developed around 2000 onward, based on the fault-primitive analysis of Topic 7 of *Memories and Their Faults*.

**March SS** (Hamdioui and co-authors, 2002) was built to detect **all static simple faults** — every single-cell and two-cell fault primitive with at most one operation:

> {⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, r0, w0, r0, w1); ⇑(r1, r1, w1, r1, w0); ⇓(r0, r0, w0, r0, w1); ⇓(r1, r1, w1, r1, w0); ⇕(r0)} — **22N**

It has the same skeleton as March C− — up, up, down, down — but every r-w pair is replaced by a richer sequence.

steps.title: 1st r0
steps.md: Checks the stored value: catches SAF, IRF, RDF — and the effects of coupling from earlier operations. If the cell has a DRDF, this read flips it without showing it.

steps.title: 2nd r0
steps.md: No write in between: the DRDF flipped by the first read is now visible.

steps.title: w0
steps.md: A **non-transition write**: the cell already holds 0. A write-disturb fault flips the cell here.

steps.title: 3rd r0
steps.md: Reads right after the non-transition write and catches the WDF.

steps.title: w1
steps.md: The 0 → 1 transition, as in March C−: it sensitizes transition faults (checked by the next element) and acts as an aggressor on cells not yet visited.

blocks.title: Twice as long, many more faults
blocks.md: March SS costs **22N** instead of 10N, and in return covers all **static** simple faults, including DRDF, WDF and the read- and write-disturb versions of coupling faults.

tabs.label: Linked faults
Dynamic faults
tabs.md:
A dynamic fault needs **two or more operations in a row** on the same cell, for example *write 1, then read 1 immediately*. Tests for them contain sequences such as **w x, r x** back to back, or several reads in a row.

Dynamic faults are timing-related: they may appear only when the operations follow each other at **full clock speed**.

tabs.label: At speed
tabs.md: Because of dynamic, recovery and precharge faults, MBIST runs memory tests at the **functional clock frequency** of the memory, not at the slow clock of a tester. This is called **at-speed** testing — one more reason to put the test hardware on the chip.

questions.text: Why does March C− miss deceptive read destructive faults (DRDF)?
options: Every read is followed by a write to the same cell before the cell is read again.
DRDF can only be found by GALPAT.

questions.text: In the March SS element ⇑(r0, r0, w0, r0, w1), which operation **sensitizes** a write-disturb fault?
options: The w0 — a write of the value the cell already holds

questions.text: How long is March SS, and what does it cover?
What must a test for linked faults do?
options: Read the victim after the first fault acts, before a second fault can undo it.

questions.text: Dynamic faults may appear only when operations follow each other at full clock speed, so MBIST runs at the memory's functional clock.
Order the tests from shortest to longest.
